metaTitle: Police Left a Card at My Door — What to Do Before You Call
metaDescription: Police left a card at my door? Verify via 101, do not discuss the allegation on the card number, and get free legal advice before you call back.
featuredImageAlt: Police calling card left at a door — what to do before you call back
contentHtml:
You came home and found a police card on the door — or a note under the mat. The urge is to ring the number and explain. Hold that thought.

In England and Wales a card left at the door is often the start of a voluntary interview under caution. It is not a casual chat. Before you call about the allegation, verify the contact and arrange free legal advice.

Key takeaways

  • If police left a card at your door, treat it as formal contact — often an invitation to a voluntary interview under caution.
  • Check the officer is real through 101. Do not rely only on the mobile or direct dial on the card.
  • Do not discuss the allegation on the phone. Take names, station and a reference. Stop there.
  • You are entitled to free legal advice before you call back about the substance. It is not means-tested for a police station interview.
  • Ignoring the card is unwise. Rearranging so a solicitor can attend is normal.

1) What a card usually means

A police calling card at the door usually means an officer wants to speak to you as a suspect or potential suspect. It may ask you to call a named PC or DC, invite you “in for a chat,” or leave a reference and station.

That pattern is common across England and Wales. It is not an arrest. It is still serious. The next step is often a booked voluntary interview under caution — recorded and usable as evidence.

For any broader invite to talk — call, letter, email or card — see The Police Want to Speak to Me. This page stays on the door-card and house-visit pattern.

2) Check the officer is real (101)

Anyone can print a card. Before you engage, verify.

Call 101 — the national non-emergency number for England and Wales. Give the force area, the officer’s name, collar or warrant number if shown, and any reference on the card. Ask the operator to confirm the officer is genuine.

Use 999 only in an emergency. Do not treat a number on the card as your first verification route. Photograph the card.

3) Do not discuss the allegation

When you speak — after verification — keep it practical.

Do not discuss the allegation on the phone. Do not give your account, timelines, alibis, apologies or guesses about phones or CCTV. Do not “clear the air.” Anything you volunteer can still be used later.

Take only: officer name and rank; collar number if given; station or unit; a verified contact route; crime reference if offered; any proposed date and place; and whether it is voluntary and under caution. Then say you will take legal advice and a solicitor will be in touch.

4) Free legal advice first

You are entitled to free and independent legal advice before a police station interview, including a voluntary interview under caution. It is not means-tested at this stage. Asking for a solicitor does not make you look guilty.

Instruct a criminal defence solicitor before you call back about the substance. Let them request disclosure, advise you in private, and rearrange so advice is in place. Do not agree a firm date until your solicitor can attend.

5) What happens next (often a voluntary interview)

Most door-card contact of this kind leads toward a voluntary interview under caution. You attend by arrangement. You are not under arrest for that attendance and may leave unless then arrested. The interview is still formal — caution, recording, same legal weight as custody questioning.

Your solicitor can advise whether to answer questions, make no comment, or use a prepared statement. There is no universal correct approach. Do not contact complainants or witnesses, and do not post about it on social media.

Kent aside (local instruction only)

If the proposed interview is in Kent or Medway, this practice can take instruction for a booked voluntary interview or current custody through Tuckers Solicitors LLP (SRA 127795). Ask for Robert Cashman, Tuckers Duty Solicitor — the DSCC have our details. Voluntary interviews · current custody. Outside Kent, instruct a local defence solicitor first.

Conclusion

If the police left a card at your door, verify via 101, do not discuss the allegation on the phone, and get free legal advice before you call back. The usual next step is a voluntary interview under caution — arrange it with a solicitor, not alone.

faq.q: The police left a card at my door — must I call the number on it?
faq.a: Verify first via 101. Do not ignore genuine contact. You do not have to discuss the allegation on the card number. Arrange free legal advice before any substantive call-back.

faq.q: Is a police calling card at my house the same as an arrest?
faq.a: No. A card is contact, not detention. An unadvised conversation can still become part of the case.

faq.q: Can I rearrange so a solicitor can attend?
faq.a: Yes. Do not simply ignore the card. Rearrange so free legal advice is in place.

faq.q: What if I already rang and explained myself?
faq.a: Stop further discussion. Instruct a solicitor now and tell them what was said. Do not try to “fix” the account on a second call.
